https://ediblemanhattan.com/resources-gu.text: Resources Guide 2 weeks ago STORY BY Christopher Pape 0 Budapest does not reveal itself slowly. Within the first hour of arriving, you are already dealing with a city that demands your full attention: the scale of the Parliament building seen from across the Danube, the thermal steam rising from ornate bath houses, the ruin bars tucked into courtyards that look abandoned until you step inside. The last thing you want mediating that first encounter is a suitcase. Most first-time visitors to Budapest arrive at Keleti, Nyugati, or Déli railway station, or at Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport, and immediately face the same problem: check-in is hours away, checkout was this morning, or the itinerary simply does not include a hotel at all. The instinct is to drag bags back to the accommodation or sit in a cafe until a room is ready. Neither option is a good use of Budapest. Drop Your Bags and Start the City Properly The practical solution is luggage storage, and Budapest has enough options that there is no reason to spend any part of your visit managing bags rather than exploring. Budapest Luggage Storage through Radical Storage connects travellers with a network of verified local shops, cafes, and businesses across the city that hold bags securely while you move freely. The process is straightforward: book online, show up at the storage location, hand over your bags, and get on with the day. Prices are transparent, the locations are spread across the city’s main neighbourhoods, and the booking confirmation gives you everything you need to drop off and collect without any uncertainty. For a city as walkable and dense as Budapest, this kind of flexibility changes the texture of the visit significantly. What to Do With a Free Day in Budapest With bags sorted, Budapest rewards exploration in a way that few European capitals can match at the same price point. The Buda Castle District is the obvious starting point for a first visit. The funicular from Clark Ádám Square delivers you to the castle plateau, where Matthias Church, Fisherman’s Bastion, and the views across the Danube to Pest justify the uphill journey entirely. The area is touristy in the way that genuinely historic places tend to be, but the architecture earns the attention. Crossing one of the bridges into Pest opens up a different energy. The Great Market Hall near Vámház körút is worth an hour regardless of whether you intend to buy anything. Three floors of Hungarian produce, paprika in every conceivable form, embroidery, and local food stalls give a concentrated sense of what the city actually eats and sells. The langos at the food stalls on the upper level is the correct lunch choice. The Jewish Quarter, centred around Dohány Street Synagogue, is one of the most layered and historically significant areas in Central Europe. The synagogue itself is the largest in Europe and worth seeing, but the streets immediately around it, which gave rise to Budapest’s ruin bar culture in the early 2000s, have developed into a neighbourhood that functions simultaneously as a cultural district, a nightlife area, and a memorial space. Szimpla Kert, the original ruin bar, is worth visiting in the afternoon when it functions more as a cafe than a venue. The thermal baths are non-negotiable for any visit longer than a day. Széchenyi in City Park is the most famous and the most photogenic, with its outdoor pools and neo-baroque architecture. Rudas on the Buda side is smaller, more atmospheric, and on weekend nights operates as a bath party that is entirely its own category of experience. Both require nothing more than a towel and a few hours. Planning Around Arrival and Departure Budapest is a city that works particularly well for travellers passing through on longer European itineraries. The train connections to Vienna, Prague, and Kraków make it a natural stop rather than a destination requiring a dedicated trip, which means many visitors arrive and depart on the same day or spend a night without a full base to work from. For these itineraries, Radical Storage makes the logistics considerably cleaner. Arriving at Keleti on a morning train, storing bags near the station, spending the day in the city, and collecting bags before an evening departure is a pattern that works smoothly when the storage infrastructure is reliable and centrally located. The same applies to travellers who have checked out of accommodation but have an afternoon flight. Rather than spending the final hours of a Budapest visit in a hotel lobby or an airport terminal, the city remains fully accessible right up to departure. A Few Practical Notes for First Visits Budapest runs on Hungarian Forints, though many central businesses accept euros at unfavourable rates. Withdrawing forints from an ATM on arrival is the straightforward approach. Public transport is excellent and inexpensive. A single transfer ticket covers metro, tram, and bus, and a 24-hour pass costs less than most single metro rides in Western European capitals. The trams along the Pest riverbank, particularly tram 2, are among the most scenic urban transit routes in Europe and worth riding simply for the view. English is widely spoken in tourist-facing businesses, less so in residential neighbourhoods, but basic Hungarian courtesies are appreciated in the way they always are when visitors make the effort. Budapest rewards the traveller who moves through it without friction. Sorting storage with Radical Storage at the start of the day is the first and simplest step toward making that possible. https://www.bursa.ro/international-georg.text: The 20th edition of the International "George Enescu” Competition began in Bucharest and runs until September 19, at a time when the Romanian capital is consolidating its role as an international center of classical music for almost a month. The anniversary edition attracted a record number of entries: 819 musicians from 58 countries entered the competition, according to information presented by the organizers. The competition is dedicated to young performers and includes violin, cello, piano and composition sections. The official opening took place at the Romanian Athenaeum, with a concert that brought together George Enescu's heritage, contemporary musical creation and the new generation of performers. The program included works by Diego Santamaria and Dan Dediu, as well as Symphony no. 1 by George Enescu. *Tradition and contemporary creation One of the distinctive elements of this year's edition is the attempt to avoid transforming the competition into a simple exercise in preserving the classical repertoire. The organizers are putting Enescu's creation face to face with works by contemporary composers, in a formula that aims to link the Romanian musical heritage with current developments on the international scene. In the opening concert, the three laureates of the previous edition - violinist Mayumi Kanagawa, cellist Yo Kitamura and pianist Roman Lopatynskyi - returned to the stage of the Romanian Athenaeum, this time as soloists, under the baton of Cristian Măcelaru and accompanied by the National Radio Orchestra. *A competition that changes generations For Romania, the importance of the competition goes beyond the dimension of a one-off cultural event. International competitions of this type function as selection platforms for the future careers of great performers. Laureates can obtain not only prizes, but also access to international concert networks, managers, cultural institutions and orchestras. Cristian Măcelaru, the artistic director of the "George Enescu” International Festival and Competition, recently stated that one of the main missions of the competition is to identify talents that can become landmarks of the international music scene. "If at the end of the competition we discover great talents, we have fulfilled one of our missions,” said the conductor, quoted on the festivalulenescu.ro website. The theme of the 2026 edition is "In search of excellence”, a concept that, according to Cristian Măcelaru, should not be seen as reaching a definitive target, but as a continuous process of training and performance. *Music also becomes an instrument of international promotion The international dimension of the competition also offers Romania a tool of cultural promotion in a field where reputation is built over the long term. This year's edition is one of the most important international competitions dedicated to young musicians and brings together both artists at the beginning of their careers and established personalities of classical music. The six symphony concerts scheduled within the competition are performed by Romanian and international orchestras, on the stage of the Romanian Athenaeum. In parallel, an international conducting masterclass coordinated by Cristian Măcelaru is taking place at the Radio Hall until August 28. The program brings together six selected young conductors and the Romanian Youth Orchestra. Thus, the contest is not limited to the competition itself, but builds a broader program of training, concerts and professional meetings. *A cultural brand that can produce economic effects For Bucharest and for Romania, an international cultural event of this size also has an indirect economic component: attracting an international audience, increasing the city's visibility and consolidating the cultural infrastructure. The experience of the previous edition of the Enescu Festival showed the potential of this brand. In 2025, the International "George Enescu" Festival brought together over 4,000 artists from 28 countries and over 100 concerts, transforming Bucharest, for four weeks, into one of the main international centers of classical music. The competition therefore has a stake that goes beyond rankings and awards. It contributes to the continuity of an internationally recognized Romanian cultural brand and creates a link between George Enescu's musical heritage and the generations that will define the classical scene in the coming decades. At a time when European cities compete not only through investments and infrastructure, but also through the ability to attract talent, audiences and international events, culture thus becomes part of the competition for visibility and symbolic capital. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqev.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tigrayan fighters have been seen on the streets of the region's main city but it is relatively quiet there as clashes flare up elsewhere By Michael Teferi BBC Africa Published 24 September 2026, 13:49 BST Updated 5 hours ago Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks from Tigrayan forces and their allies in parts of the north of the country, in its first statement since fighting broke out on Wednesday. The army said hostilities began in an area of Amhara region close to the border with Tigray, adding that its soldiers had inflicted heavy casualties and seized weapons. The developments come as tensions between the federal government and Tigrayan leaders have sharply escalated over the last few days, raising fears that a devastating civil war could resume. On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports from federal police. The TPLF has not commented on the army's claims and the BBC has not been able to independently verify the army's claims. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told AFP news agency on Thursday that Tigrayan forces had launched heavy artillery attacks as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the border with Tigray. "We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice-president Amanuel Assefa is quoted by the news agency as saying. The latest escalation follows months of rising tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and Tigray authorities, who fought a devastating war from 2020 to 2022. That ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating the agreement. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday. This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days. A Mekelle resident told the BBC's Newsday programme on Thursday there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere. Figure caption, Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates "Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash. "People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash." Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash". With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC.
